chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from an-Nadr and Fadalah from Ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

"For every prayer there are two times, and the first of the two times is the more virtuous: the time of Fajr prayer is when the dawn breaks until the morning covers the sky, and it is not appropriate to delay it intentionally, but it is the time for one who is busy or forgets or errs or sleeps. And the time of Maghrib prayer is when the sun sets until the stars become intermingled, and no one should make the last of the two times the [primary] time except due to an excuse or a reason."

Al-Sheikh (may Allah have mercy on him) said: And for each of the five obligatory prayers there are two times, a first and a last; the first is for one who has no excuse, and the second is for those with excuses. And it is not appropriate for anyone to delay the prayer from its first time while he is mindful of it and not prevented from it. If he delays it and then is cut off [by death or sleep] in the time before he performs it, he is one who has neglected it. And if he remains until he performs it in the last time or between the first and the last, he is excused for his sin in delaying it. We have clarified previously that the last time is the time for the one with an excuse and need, and that for one who has no excuse, his time is the first time. And this is also confirmed by what he narrated:
ai.seo_question: What are the preferred and last times for daily prayers in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi elaborates that the 'first time' serves as the obligatory window for those with no excuse, while the 'last time' is reserved for those with valid impediments, establishing a clear hierarchy of diligence. This distinction underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that delaying prayer without cause constitutes negligence (muḍayyiʿ), whereas doing so due to necessity is excused, reinforcing the balance between strict adherence and practical flexibility in worship.
